Agamemnon. The king of Mycenae and supreme commander of the Greek forces at Troy, he led the thousand-ship expedition against the Trojans to reclaim his brother's wife Helen. To secure favorable winds for the voyage, he sacrificed his own daughter Iphigenia to the goddess Artemis, an act that would haunt him for the rest of his life. Once at Troy, Agamemnon ruled with absolute authority over all the allied kingdoms, yet his pride and poor judgment brought disaster upon the Greeks. He clashed repeatedly with Achilles over war prizes and honor, nearly destroying Greek unity itself. When he claimed the captive Briseis as his war prize, Achilles withdrew from battle in rage, a crisis that prolonged the war and cost countless lives. After inheriting the throne of Mycenae from his father Atreus, Agamemnon might have ruled peacefully, but instead he led the Greeks through a decade of brutal conflict. His return home ended in tragedy when his wife Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus murdered him in revenge for Iphigenia's sacrifice. Agamemnon stands as the central dramatic focus of the Iliad, where his leadership, his quarrels, and ultimately his fatal pride shape the entire course of the war.
